analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to let passengers off planes stuck on the tarmac after three hours, with food, water, and medical access.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died when the 111th Congress ended, though the Transportation Department later imposed a similar three-hour tarmac rule by regulation in 2010.
analysis.plain_summary: The Airline Passenger Bill of Rights Act of 2009 would have required every airline and airport to file a plan with the Transportation Department for handling long tarmac delays. Airlines would have had to provide food, water, working restrooms, ventilation, and medical care to passengers stuck on a grounded plane, and offer passengers the option to get off after three hours, with narrow exceptions for safety. Airports would have had to explain how they would return people to the terminal and make gates available. Airlines or airports that failed to follow an approved plan could be fined, and the Transportation Department would have set up a consumer hotline for passenger complaints. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers stuck on planes held on the ground for hours without food, water, or a way to get off. The bill covered both departing and arriving flights, including flights diverted to a different airport. It would also have created a government hotline for passenger complaints and made each airline's delay plan public.

how_it_helps.text: Airlines must provide passengers on a delayed grounded aircraft with adequate food, potable water, restroom facilities, cabin ventilation, and access to necessary medical treatment.

After three hours on the ground with the doors closed, passengers must be given the option to deplane and return to the terminal, offered at least once every successive three-hour period, unless the pilot determines departure or unloading is within 30 minutes or that deplaning would jeopardize safety or security.
The rules apply whether a plane is held before takeoff or after landing, and apply to diverted flights at airports other than the original destination.
Airports must file plans describing how passengers will be deplaned after a long tarmac delay and how facilities will be shared and gates made available for delayed aircraft.

The Secretary of Transportation may assess civil penalties against carriers or airport operators that fail to submit, obtain approval of, or adhere to a contingency plan, and each approved plan must be publicly accessible.
The bill directs the Secretary to establish a consumer hotline telephone number for air passenger complaints.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which would bear the cost of providing food, water, and gate access during delays and face civil penalties for failing to follow approved plans, costs that are likely to be passed on to ticket prices to some degree. Airport operators also face planning obligations, penalties, and pressure to make gates and facilities available for delayed aircraft.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires a deplaning option after three hours but allows the pilot to skip it if the aircraft will depart or be unloaded within 30 minutes or if deplaning would jeopardize passenger safety or security, exceptions that give airlines flexibility to keep passengers on board.

Compliance costs fall on airlines and airports, and hard deadlines can push carriers toward canceling flights rather than risking multi-hour holds, a tradeoff carriers have historically argued against tarmac delay rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to passengers is concrete: food, water, working restrooms, and a way off a plane after three hours instead of an open-ended wait, backed by fines and a public complaint hotline. The main costs are compliance expenses for airlines and airports and the risk that rigid time limits lead to more flight cancellations, which the pilot exceptions in the bill were designed to soften. On balance the protections are narrow and targeted at a well-known failure mode of air travel, and the passenger benefit clearly outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee on the day it was introduced, no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and it died there when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson introduced the Airline Passenger Bill of Rights Act of 2009 in the House on January 21, 2009.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and, the next day, to its Subcommittee on Aviation.
Thirty-six members cosponsored the bill, including 31 Democrats and 5 Republicans, but the bill never advanced past its subcommittee referral.
The bill's complete action history ends with the subcommittee referral; no committee vote, floor action, or roll call ever occurred.

Separately, the Transportation Department issued its own rule in 2010 requiring airlines to let passengers deplane after three hours on the tarmac and to provide food and water, delivering much of what the bill sought through regulation rather than legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines and airport operators are better off because the bill never became law: they avoided statutory food, water, and three-hour deplaning requirements and civil penalties, at least for the two years the bill sat in committee. Passengers ultimately got a similar three-hour rule anyway, but through the Transportation Department's 2010 regulation rather than this statute.

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Airline Passenger Bill of Rights Act of 2009 on January 21, 2009.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never took the bill up; the complete action history shows no markup, vote, or further action after the subcommittee referral.

against.name: U.S. passenger airlines
against.role: Industry subject to the bill's requirements and penalties
against.what_they_did: Opposed statutory tarmac-delay mandates during this era, arguing time limits would cause more cancellations, and the legislative approach was superseded by the Transportation Department's own 2010 rule.

sides.party_line_note: The 36 cosponsors split 31 Democrats and 5 Republicans, and the bill's opponents were the committee's inaction and the airline industry rather than one party.

industries.note: Airlines would have had to provide food, water, restrooms, ventilation, and medical access during tarmac delays, offer deplaning after three hours, file public contingency plans, and face civil penalties for noncompliance. Passengers stuck on a plane are the direct counterpart to the airline's cost of ending the hold, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against travelers.

Airports would have had to file approved plans for deplaning delayed aircraft and for sharing facilities and making gates available, subject to civil penalties. Their interest in keeping gates open for scheduled flights ran against stranded passengers waiting to get off a plane.
